interactions.summary: Jiang says European anti-Semitism grows out of the unresolved Christian history he has just described, and he casts Dante's genius as the ability to reconcile that convoluted history into a philosophy that moves readers closer to God.

A student asks whether Dante believes Jesus is God and how far he agrees with the Catholic Church, and Jiang answers with a speculative reading: because open heresy could be fatal, Dante stays subtle, but Jiang guesses Dante saw Jesus as a divinely inspired spiritual leader rather than as unique in divinity.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Student question with Jiang speculative answer

interactions.summary: Another student asks whether Jiang's prior account of Jesus's death was meant as factual history or biblical doctrine, and Jiang clarifies that he is summarizing official Catholic teaching rather than asserting its truth.

Jiang says that to understand Jesus's essence the class should read the poetic core of the Bible, the Sermon on the Mount, which he treats as divinely inspired in a way comparable to the Divine Comedy.
A student begins reading the Beatitudes from the Gospel of Matthew as the selected passage through which Jiang wants the class to encounter Jesus's voice.

claims.claim: Jiang says the unresolved Christian history around Jesus and the Jews has produced major evil in Europe, explicitly naming anti-Semitism as an outcome Dante feels compelled to reconcile.
Jiang says Dante's genius lies in taking a complex and convoluted religious history and turning it into a philosophy people can appreciate and act upon in order to move closer to God.
Jiang says we can never fully know Dante's true theological beliefs because in Dante's period a person could be killed for heresy, forcing subtle and nuanced expression.

Jiang's own guess is that Dante saw Jesus as a great spiritual leader who was divine in nature, but not uniquely so, since Jiang analogizes Jesus's inspiration to Dante writing under divine possession as well.

Jiang says the prior account of Jesus, crucifixion, and Jewish punishment was not his own truth claim but a simplified presentation of official Catholic teaching that Justinian will repeat in the text.
Jiang says that if one wants the essence of Jesus, the most revealing biblical passage is poetic, the Sermon on the Mount, which he places beside the Divine Comedy as divinely inspired speech.
The passage chosen to reveal Jesus is the opening Beatitudes from Matthew, emphasizing poverty of spirit, mourning, meekness, mercy, purity, peacemaking, and persecution for righteousness.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang says Dante had to hide his deepest theology behind subtlety because open heresy could get him killed.
signature_moments.source_phrase: you could be killed for defying the catholic church
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It reframes interpretation of Dante as reading under pressure, where nuance is not ornament but survival strategy.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang speculates that Dante would treat both Jesus and Dante as figures through whom God takes possession in order to deliver a saving message.
signature_moments.source_phrase: god has taken possession of me
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is a strong interpretive wager that collapses the distance between prophetic speech and poetic speech inside Jiang's reading of Dante.

signature_moments.moment: To get Jesus's essence, Jiang turns not to doctrine but to poetry, treating the Sermon on the Mount as divinely inspired speech comparable to the Divine Comedy.
signature_moments.source_phrase: there is a part of the bible that is poetry
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It makes poetry the privileged medium for spiritual truth in both Christianity and Dante, which is one of Jiang's deepest recurring commitments.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: The charge that, in Jiang's account, could get a medieval writer killed, forcing Dante's theological disagreement into subtle and indirect form.
The poetic biblical passage Jiang selects as the best access point to Jesus's essence and divinely inspired voice.
The opening blessings from Matthew that the class reads as the first concrete presentation of Jesus after Jiang's historical framing.

chronology_notes.note: This 2026-06-16 packet shifts from the official Catholic history into Jiang's first explicit statement about how to read Dante's relation to Jesus: historical caution because of heresy, interpretive speculation about divine inspiration, and then a move into the Sermon on the Mount as Jesus's poetic core.

uncertainty_notes.note: Jiang marks his view of Dante's theology here as an explicit guess rather than as a claim directly grounded in Dante's stated doctrine, so the packet should preserve that speculation instead of hardening it into certainty.
The transcript's 'sermon on the mouth' is an ASR distortion of the Sermon on the Mount, but the intended biblical reference is clear from context and the immediately following Matthew reading.
